title: The Union Legislature
tagline: Two Houses, one Parliament: composition, sessions, procedure and the powers that make law at the centre.

overview.intro: The Union Legislature is the law-making arm of the Union government and the clearest expression of the federal idea in the Constitution: one House represents the people directly and the other represents the States, and both must normally agree before a law is passed. This chapter works through the composition and qualifications of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, the vocabulary of parliamentary procedure that examiners ask for by name — session, quorum, question hour, starred and unstarred questions, zero hour, adjournment and no-confidence motions — and then the powers that belong to Parliament as a whole, including the one that only one House can exercise on its own.

facts.label: Lok Sabha
facts.value: The directly elected House; maximum 550 members, term five years unless dissolved sooner.

facts.label: Rajya Sabha
facts.value: The Council of States; maximum 250 members, a permanent House with one third retiring every two years.

facts.label: Quorum
facts.value: One tenth of the total membership of the House must be present before it can transact business.

facts.label: No-confidence motion
facts.value: Only the Lok Sabha can pass one, and it alone can remove the Council of Ministers.

learningOutcomes: Describe the composition, term and mode of election of the two Houses and the qualifications for membership.
Explain the working of a session: prorogation and dissolution, the presidential address, question hour and zero hour.
Distinguish the kinds of questions, motions and bills, including why a money bill is special.
State the legislative, financial, judicial, electoral and amendatory powers of Parliament and the exclusive powers of each House.
Write a short-answer account of the Speaker and the anti-defection provisions with the correct article references.

learn.title: The two Houses: composition, election and qualifications

blocks.text: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses, and the President is part of Parliament even though the President does not sit in either chamber. The Lok Sabha is elected directly by adult citizens on the basis of universal adult franchise from territorial constituencies, and its normal life is five years, though it may be dissolved earlier by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The Rajya Sabha is elected indirectly by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies by the system of proportional representation with a single transferable vote, and because one third of its members retire every two years it is a continuing House that is never dissolved. Both Houses have similar law-making powers, but only the directly elected House reflects a general election result, which is why the government of the day is answerable to it.

items: Lok Sabha: maximum strength 550, elected from States and Union Territories; the provision for nominated Anglo-Indian members was repealed by the 104th Amendment Act, 2020.
Rajya Sabha: maximum strength 250 — up to 238 elected from States and Union Territories and 12 members nominated by the President for distinction in literature, science, art and social service.
A member of either House must be a citizen of India and take an oath of allegiance to the Constitution before sitting or voting.
Minimum ages: 25 years for the Lok Sabha and 30 years for the Rajya Sabha, which is a favourite one-mark distinction.

items.note: Because only one third of its members retire every two years, the House never stands empty, so Parliament can sit even in the interval after a general election.

items.note: An advocate of ten years standing in a High Court qualifies for the Rajya Sabha, while the Lok Sabha candidate simply needs the minimum age of 25 years.

learn.title: Sessions, presiding officers and the daily routine

blocks.text: The life of the Lok Sabha is divided into sessions, prorogations and adjournments, and the three words mean quite different things. A session opens with the President’s address to a joint sitting, in which the government sets out its programme. Adjournment merely suspends business for a short period; prorogation ends the session; dissolution brings the House itself to an end. Business begins with question hour, the first hour of the sitting, when members put questions to ministers and the answers are given orally or laid on the table. Zero hour follows question hour and is an Indian innovation: members raise matters of urgent public importance without notice. A House cannot act at all unless a quorum, one tenth of its membership, is present, and when it falls short the Speaker or Chairman rings the bell and, if the House is still short, may adjourn it.

items: Question hour: the first hour of a sitting, devoted to questions for which twenty-four hours’ notice is given.

Starred questions are answered orally and allow supplementary questions; unstarred questions are answered in writing with no supplementary; short-notice questions are answered orally with less than the ordinary notice period, at the Speaker’s leave.
Zero hour follows question hour and is not covered by the rules, which is exactly what makes it flexible.
The Speaker is elected from among the members of the Lok Sabha and presides over its sittings; the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

The Speaker is the final authority on the interpretation of the rules of the House and certifies a money bill, a certificate that was held final in the Kesavananda-era practice and by the Supreme Court.

items.note: A member asks the Railways Minister about train punctuality, the minister replies from the box, and the member may then press two or three supplementary questions.
With 54 members present in a House of 545, the business cannot proceed; the bell is rung, and if members still do not come in the sitting may be adjourned.

The minimum number of members who must be present before the House may transact business, one tenth of the total.
A motion asking the House to sit for a limited time to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, whose acceptance requires the majority present and voting.

learn.title: Motions, bills and the special position of the money bill

blocks.text: A motion is a proposal made to the House so that it may take a decision, and the names examiners ask for are the budget motion, the cut motion, the no-confidence motion and the adjournment motion. The no-confidence motion is the constitutional check on the executive: it may be moved only in the Lok Sabha, needs the support of at least fifty members for leave, and if it is passed the Council of Ministers must resign or advise a dissolution. The cut motion is a financial device that seeks to reduce a demand for grants; a policy cut asks for a rupee, a token cut is meant to draw attention to a matter of public importance, and an economy cut proposes a specific amount of reduction. When a bill has passed both Houses and been presented, the President may assent, withhold assent, or return the bill for reconsideration — except for a money bill, which the President may not return.

items: Ordinary bills may originate in either House and must pass both; a joint sitting under Article 108 can break a deadlock, and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides at that joint sitting.
A money bill deals only with the matters listed in Article 110 and can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the President’s recommendation.
The Rajya Sabha may keep a money bill for at most fourteen days, after which it is deemed to have been passed even if it does not agree.
A financial bill is not a money bill: it involves expenditure but also other provisions, so it follows the ordinary route.

The anti-defection provisions of the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985, disqualify a member who voluntarily gives up the membership of the party or votes against its whip, with an exception when two thirds of the party group merge with another.

learn.title: The powers of Parliament as a whole

blocks.text: Parliament exercises legislative power by making law on the Union and concurrent lists and, within limits, on matters of national importance; financial power by controlling the executive’s spending, since no tax may be levied and no money spent without the authority of law and a vote of the House; judicial power in the narrow form of trying and removing the President and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts; electoral power in choosing the President and Vice-President; and the amendatory power of Article 368, by which Parliament may add, change or repeal provisions of the Constitution subject to the basic structure that the courts have read into it. Parliament also holds the executive to account through questions, debates, cut motions and the confidence requirement itself. The exclusive powers separate the Houses: only the Lok Sabha has the no-confidence power, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to it, and it alone may introduce a money bill; the Rajya Sabha alone can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State subject by a two-thirds majority.

items: Legislative power: law-making on the Union List and the Concurrent List, where a Union law prevails over a State law on the same subject.
Financial power: the annual financial statement is laid before the Lok Sabha, demands for grants are voted, and the Appropriation Bill and Finance Bill follow.
Judicial power: impeachment of the President and removal proceedings against judges, which are quasi-judicial functions of Parliament.
Electoral power: the elected members of both Houses and the elected members of the Assemblies together form the Electoral College for the President.
Amendatory power: Article 368 permits amendment by a two-thirds majority of each House and ratification by half the States for changes touching certain List entries.

items.note: The Speaker certifies the bill, the Rajya Sabha reports within fourteen days, and on the President’s assent it becomes an Act, all without a joint sitting.
An ordinary bill sent back for reconsideration must be passed again; if the Houses hold to it the President may still assent, because assent cannot ultimately be refused forever.

items.meaning: A bill restricted to the matters in Article 110, introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President’s recommendation and not returnable by the Rajya Sabha.
A sitting of both Houses presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha to resolve a deadlock, convened by the President under Article 108.
The obligation of the Council of Ministers to stand or fall together with the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
The Tenth Schedule rules that disqualify a member who defects or votes against the party whip, subject to the two-thirds merger exception.
The deciding vote the Speaker or Chairman may give when the House is equally divided, other than on a matter requiring a majority of total membership.

learn.title: Writing answers on the Union Legislature

blocks.text: Questions on this unit are usually of three kinds: a distinguish pair, a describe question worth ten marks, and a short note. For a distinguish pair, the fastest reliable structure is one line of contrast per feature in two columns, never two paragraphs in prose. For a ten-mark description, open with a definition, then organise the body under the headings the question names, quote one article for each constitutional feature, and close with one sentence on why the feature matters to the working of democracy. Numbers carry marks: remember the maximum strengths, the minimum ages, the one-tenth quorum, the fourteen days allowed to the Rajya Sabha on a money bill and the two-thirds majorities. Finally, practise naming the article that the question is silently asking for, because the marker’s scheme usually contains it.

items: For a distinguish question, one contrast per row; for a describe question, definition, ordered body, one article each, and a closing sentence of significance.
Never write the wrong House: no-confidence, money bills and collective responsibility are Lok Sabha matters; the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha.
Quote the article only when sure of it — Article 83 duration, Article 100 quorum, Article 108 joint sitting, Article 110 money bill, Article 112 financial statement.
Numbers earn marks: 550, 250, 12 nominated, 25 and 30 years, one third retiring, fourteen days, one tenth quorum.

keyPoints: Parliament means the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha together.
The Lok Sabha is directly elected with a maximum of 550 members and a five-year term; the Rajya Sabha has a maximum of 250 and is never dissolved.
Rajya Sabha members are elected by MLAs by proportional representation with a single transferable vote, and 12 members are nominated by the President.
Minimum age is 25 for the Lok Sabha and 30 for the Rajya Sabha; both require an oath of allegiance.
A session begins with the President’s address; adjournment suspends, prorogation ends the session and dissolution ends the House.
Question hour is the first hour; starred questions allow supplementaries, unstarred are written, short-notice gets reduced notice.
Zero hour follows question hour, needs no notice and is an Indian innovation.
Quorum is one tenth of the total membership; the Speaker certifies a money bill and is the final authority on the rules.
A money bill can start only in the Lok Sabha, only on the President’s recommendation, and the Rajya Sabha may keep it only fourteen days.
Only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion, and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to it alone.
Parliament holds legislative, financial, judicial, electoral and amendatory powers; Article 368 governs amendment.
The Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment, 1985, deals with disqualification for defection.
examFocus: Distinguish questions in this chapter are almost always the same pairs: starred and unstarred, adjournment and prorogation, money bill and financial bill, cut motion and no-confidence motion.
Ten-mark descriptions ask for composition or powers — write them in ordered headings and attach one article to each constitutional feature.
Numbers are marked: quote the strengths, ages, quorum fraction and the fourteen-day and two-thirds rules precisely.

vocabulary.meaning: The territorial area from which one member is elected to the Lok Sabha.
The party instruction to members on how to vote, breach of which attracts disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
A question answered orally in the House that permits supplementary questions.
The unscheduled period after question hour for urgent matters raised without notice.
A bill confined to Article 110 subjects, with special introduction, passage and assent rules.
The parliamentary procedure for removing the President on a charge of violating the Constitution.
A law promulgated by the President when Parliament is not in session, which must be laid before Parliament and lapses in six weeks.
A motion to reduce a demand for grants, used to test the government’s policy or finances.

questions.prompt: The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is:
questions.explanation: Article 330 as amended fixes the strength at up to 550 members elected from States and Union Territories.

questions.prompt: The quorum to transact business in either House is:
questions.explanation: Article 100 requires one tenth of the total membership of the House to be present.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an exclusive power of the Lok Sabha?
questions.explanation: Only the Lok Sabha may pass a no-confidence motion; the other three are functions of Parliament or the Electoral College as a whole.

questions.prompt: A bill certified by the Speaker as a money bill must be returned by the Rajya Sabha within:
questions.explanation: If the Rajya Sabha does not report within fourteen days, the bill is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.

questions.prompt: The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio __________ of the Rajya Sabha.
questions.explanation: The Vice-President presides over the Council of States without being a member of it.

questions.prompt: A motion asking the House to reduce a demand for grant by a stated amount is called a cut __________.
questions.explanation: The cut motion is the financial instrument for challenging a demand for grants.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a starred question and an unstarred question.
questions.answer: A starred question is answered orally in the House during the prescribed hour and is followed by supplementary questions, which need no notice; an unstarred question is answered in writing, the answer is laid on the table or published, and no supplementary question may be asked on it.
questions.explanation: The oral answer with supplementaries against the written answer without them is the whole of the distinction.

questions.prompt: What is a quorum? What happens if it is not present when a sitting begins?
questions.answer: A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present before the House may transact any business, fixed at one tenth of the total membership of the House by Article 100. If the Speaker or Chairman finds the quorum absent, a bell is rung to bring members in; if they still do not come, the sitting is adjourned or suspended until a quorum is present.
questions.explanation: One tenth is the constitutional figure, and the ringing of the bell followed by adjournment is the prescribed procedure.

questions.prompt: State two powers that belong to the Rajya Sabha alone.
questions.answer: First, it may authorise Parliament by a resolution passed by two thirds of its members present and voting to make laws on a subject in the State List. Second, it has a delaying role of its own: on an ordinary bill it may keep the bill for a maximum of six months and return it, forcing a joint sitting.
questions.explanation: The State-list resolution is the Rajya Sabha’s unique legislative power, and the six-month delay is its unique procedural power.

questions.prompt: Describe the procedure for the passage of an ordinary bill and explain how a deadlock between the two Houses is resolved.
questions.answer: A bill may be introduced in either House, except a money bill, which can begin only in the Lok Sabha on the President’s recommendation. It is read a second time, when its provisions are considered clause by clause and amendments or reference to a standing committee may be made, and then read a third time and passed by a majority of members present and voting. The other House repeats the same three readings. If both Houses pass the identical text it goes to the President for assent. If they disagree, the President may set up a joint sitting of both Houses under Article 108; the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides, the matter is decided by a simple majority of the members present and voting in both Houses taken together, and that decision is final. The joint sitting procedure does not apply to money bills, because the Rajya Sabha’s role there is limited to a fourteen-day return.
questions.explanation: Three readings in each House, presidential assent, and an Article 108 joint sitting presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker as the deadlock-breaking device.

questions.prompt: Explain the anti-defection provisions of the Constitution, giving the amendment that introduced them.
questions.answer: The provisions are contained in the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985. A member of a House is disqualified if the member voluntarily gives up the membership of the political party on whose ticket the member was elected, or if the member votes or abstains from voting contrary to any direction issued by the party whip without obtaining the party’s permission. There is an exception where two thirds of the members of the party group have merged with another party, in which case those members are not disqualified. The decision on a question of disqualification is referred to the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha or the Speaker of the Lok Sabha as the case may be, and may be challenged before the High Court and the Supreme Court. The schedule exists to stop the practice of floor-crossing that destabilised State governments in the 1960s.
questions.explanation: Tenth Schedule, two grounds of disqualification, the two-thirds merger exception and the authority deciding the question.

questions.prompt: A member crosses the floor after being elected on a party ticket and the party issues a whip for a budget vote. The member votes against the whip. Analyse whether the member is disqualified, and state who decides the question.
questions.answer: The member is prima facie disqualified: voting against a direction issued by the party without the party’s permission is one of the two grounds in paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule. Two qualifications must be checked before concluding. First, the exception in paragraph 4 applies only if two thirds of the members of the party group have merged with another party, which ordinary floor-crossing by an individual does not achieve. Second, the member may claim that the direction was never issued or that permission was given, which is a factual defence. The question of disqualification is decided by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and since the Supreme Court held in Kihoto Hollohan that the Speaker’s decision is subject to judicial review, the member may approach the High Court and then the Supreme Court if the decision appears to violate the schedule itself.
questions.explanation: The disqualification is triggered by the vote against whip, subject to the merger exception and any permission defence, and it is decided by the presiding officer subject to judicial review.
